input_format: citation. retrieval_title. retrieval_summary. authority_class. legal_regime. raw_text

scenarios.query: We've set up a utilities dynamic market for our maintenance work and want to award a contract to companies already inside it. Do we still need to publish a normal public tender notice for this award, or does a different process apply to notifying the market members?

One of our bidders has a documented history of failing to meet contract standards for another NHS body, even after being given a chance to improve. Can we take that into account when deciding whether this supplier can compete for our contract, and separately, is there a route for that kind of track record to lead to the supplier being barred from public contracts more broadly?

We want to alert the market early about a big IT procurement that's still months away from going out to tender, so suppliers have time to prepare. Is publishing that kind of early notice something we're required to do, and what would we need to include in it?
Is it actually allowed for us to score bids purely on price and ignore quality altogether, or do we always have to build in some kind of non-price scoring criteria?

Before we go out to market on this one, do we actually have to stop and think about splitting it into smaller packages to give smaller firms a chance, or can we just carry on letting it as one big contract like we always have?

This contract is well above the usual reporting threshold - are we legally required to set specific measurable performance indicators for it no matter what, or is there any get-out if the kind of work just doesn't lend itself to that kind of scoring?

A bidder has a well-documented history of seriously underperforming on a previous public contract, even though nobody sued them over it or got a court ruling. Are we allowed to factor that track record into whether they can take part in our competition, and if so, what do we need to be able to show?
Is there a government-wide list of suppliers who are barred from all public contracts, and are we required to check it before we sign, or does exclusion only ever operate competition-by-competition?

Once we've picked a winning bidder, is there a mandatory waiting period we must observe before we can sign the contract, how long is it, and are there any situations where we can go straight to signature without waiting?
Can we switch straight to a direct award with a supplier of our choosing after a competitive procedure produced no suitable tenders, and if so what do we need to check or publish before we go ahead?

Is there a hard cap on how long a new framework can run, and if we want to go beyond the usual limit because of the nature of what we're buying, is there anything specific we need to record or publish?
Can we deliberately structure these as separate smaller purchases to stay under the threshold, and if we do have a genuinely below-threshold contract, what do we still need to publish?

We're about to award a contract worth roughly £18,000 to a consultancy without running a full competition, since it's a small piece of work that's well below the usual procurement threshold. Before we go ahead, do we still have any publication or notice duties under the Procurement Act, or does the Act simply not apply once you're below the main threshold figure?

We have a staffing framework that's coming up to its expiry date, and we'd like to just extend it for another couple of years rather than re-running the whole competition, since it's working well operationally. Is there a hard statutory limit on how long a framework like this can run, or can we extend it by agreement if both sides are willing?

We've had an FOI request asking for full copies of the tenders in an ongoing procurement, including a bidder's pricing, which they've told us is commercially sensitive. Can we withhold that information, and what would we need to be able to show if the requester or the bidder challenged our decision?

We're about to enter into a £6.2 million grounds maintenance contract. What should our ongoing key performance indicator process look like once the contract is live -- how many KPIs do we need, and how often do we need to assess and publish performance against them?

We want to set up an internal process for monitoring and reporting on payment performance across our contracts and their supply chains. What information do we need to track, and how often do we need to publish it, to stay compliant?

We're considering setting up a rolling pool of pre-qualified suppliers for repeat minor works, rather than re-tendering every time. What's the practical process for establishing this and keeping the supplier list compliant over time, including what we need to do if a supplier on the list later becomes an excluded supplier?

Is there an actual statutory route for a supplier to challenge being placed on the debarment list, with a defined time limit and remedy, or is that just something people describe informally? I need the real legal mechanism here, not a summary from a blog.

One of our framework suppliers wants an 18-month extension on their call-off contract because of supply problems, and separately we're wondering whether we can just extend the framework itself rather than re-competing it when it reaches its original end date. Are either of those changes allowed without a new procurement, and how far could we realistically go?

A supplier on one of our contracts keeps missing the performance targets we set, even after we've raised it with them and given them a chance to sort it out. Can we terminate for that on its own, and separately, do we have any obligation to report or publish anything about the poor performance?

We think only one supplier can realistically deliver this specialist research contract, so we're planning to award it directly without competition. What do we need to publish before we actually sign the contract with them?

We've picked our preferred bidder for a highways contract after running a full competitive tender. What do we need to publish to record that decision, and do we owe the unsuccessful bidders any kind of individual feedback before we publish it?

Our main contractor is dragging its heels paying its subcontractors on this scheme - do the prompt payment rules we imposed on the main contract actually reach down to protect the subcontractors too, and do the subcontractors have any separate right to charge interest on the late amounts?

Can we build a meaningful chunk of the scoring around whether bidders will commit to paying the real living wage to the staff working on this contract, or would that be going beyond what we're allowed to assess tenders on?

One of our bidders is currently the subject of a central inquiry that could eventually see them barred from all public contracts, but that hasn't been decided yet and they're not on any published list. Do we have to wait for that process to finish before we can make our own call on this bidder, or can we act now within our own competition?
Given how urgent and unavoidable this is, can we award a contract directly without competing it, and does the usual wait before we're allowed to sign the contract still apply in a case like this?

Now that a challenge has formally been issued and we've been notified of it during this waiting period, are we still free to go ahead with the change, and how does that interact with the standstill period we already gave?

We awarded this contract a couple of years before the new Procurement Act rules came in, and it doesn't expire for a while yet. The company delivering it has just changed ownership, and the new structure looks like something that would count against them if they were bidding today. Does that ownership change give us a right to terminate the contract now, or are we limited to whatever termination grounds applied under the rules that were in force when we ran the original competition?

We have a below-threshold consultancy contract that we'd like to extend by six months and add a bit of extra scope, and the change would still leave it comfortably under the value where it would count as a full public contract. Do we need to justify this change against one of the Act's formal modification grounds, the same way we would for one of our larger contracts, or is there more flexibility for a contract of this size?

We ran a full competitive tender for a bespoke system, but none of the bids we received were usable -- some failed our mandatory requirements and we also have concerns about coordinated pricing between two bidders. We're under real time pressure. Can we move to a direct award without starting a fresh competition, and if so, what do we need to check and publish before we do?

We've just published our contract award notice - is there a legally required waiting period before we're allowed to actually sign the contract, or can we go ahead now that bidders have been told the outcome? If there is a wait, how long is it and what's the actual legal basis, not just what my colleague assumes?
Will pipeline notices need to be published for each financial year?
In terms of communications for pre-market engagement, will this still be electronic, and are there any exceptions?
If a potential contract meets or exceeds a relevant threshold, does the contracting authority have to use one of the prescribed procedures?
In what instances would you be able to modify award criteria?
Can a framework be opened to new suppliers without changing the terms at all?
Can we still use a selection questionnaire in an Open Framework?
Will standstill notices apply to direct awards under a framework?
For a Dynamic Market, must all call-off tenders or mini-competitions be openly advertised even though participation is limited to suppliers appointed to the Dynamic Market?
Section 22 of the Act states that the criteria may assess legal or financial capacity OR technical ability. Could this also be AND, so that criteria assess both?
Does the new contract subject matter need to be the same as or closely related to the bad performance or contract performance notice if considering exclusion?
Is it mandatory for every supplier to be registered on the Central Digital Platform?
When designing a competitive flexible process, when would suppliers get the opportunity to state their case before being removed from the tender?
Is there a legal way to fairly evaluate local suppliers, for example suppliers from your city or county?
Does the assessment summary requirement apply to under-threshold tenders?
Can the new standstill period be paused, extended, or restarted to deal with potential supplier challenges?
Does publication of the Contract Award Notice constitute day one or day zero of the standstill period?
What notice requirements apply to below-threshold tenders?
To what extent can an existing contract be modified to allow for a reduced service and cost reduction during the life of the contract?
Are the Schedule 8 safe-harbours that require details in a tender or transparency notice available for modifications to a call-off contract from a framework?
How many days before making a change does the Contract Change Notice need to be submitted?
Would a Contract Change Notice be required if the change is de minimis but still brings the contract over threshold?
We called the contract off from a framework agreement. We don't need to publish details, do we?
Can we renew an existing contract on exactly the same terms without having to run the procurement process all over again?
We want to vary the terms of our contract with a supplier. Can we do this without having to run the procurement process all over again?
We want to extend our contract with a supplier so that it runs on the same terms for an extra two years. Can we do this without having to run the procurement process all over again?
We need to extend the contract because the current supplier is the only one that can deliver the service. Is this permissible?
Do we have to keep records about the procurement?
What information must our advertisement include?
How should I calculate contract value for the purposes of advertising a framework agreement?
Do we have to advertise contracts under the relevant threshold?
Can my organisation use a framework that someone else set up?
Do we have to provide in the contract documents an exhaustive list of all contracting authorities who will potentially use the framework?
We want to set up a framework agreement but don't see how we can specify all the main terms of individual call-off contracts in advance - is this a problem?
If a framework agreement is declared ineffective, does that mean the call-off contracts are also ineffective?
Separate SQ stage for under-threshold contract - No longer possible?
Is there a requirement to publish our SQ anywhere?
Shall we disclose our SQ scoring system in the tender documentation?
When should we consider using the competitive dialogue procedure or competitive procedure with negotiation?
What are the timeframes for each procedure?
Can we abandon a procurement following receipt of bids?
What counts as the first and last day of the standstill period?
The contract is for a Light Touch Regime service. Do we have to observe a standstill period?

For an IT services contract we're about to tender under the Procurement Act 2023, can we require bidders to hold Cyber Essentials certification before we'll award the contract, and what's the legal basis for imposing that kind of requirement?

We're drafting a services contract and want to avoid the kind of disproportionate risk transfer and unlimited liability clauses suppliers keep complaining about. What does government procurement policy say we should be doing at this stage of the deal?

A long-standing supplier is citing cashflow problems again and is asking us to apply the COVID-19 supplier relief measures under PPN 02/20 so we keep paying them regardless of delivery. Can we still rely on that policy today?

We're planning a major shipbuilding procurement and are worried that open competitive tendering under the Procurement Act 2023 could expose sensitive capability information or entrench a foreign-dependent supply chain. Can we simply take the whole contract outside the Act on national security grounds, and what should we do first?

We act for a disappointed bidder who wants to challenge a contract award decision made by a central government department under the new procurement regime. They also think it may be worth issuing a parallel judicial review claim just in case. What time limit governs the statutory challenge, and if we issue in both the Administrative Court and the specialist procurement court at the same time, which court actually ends up hearing the case?

A losing bidder has issued proceedings during our standstill period, which means we're now automatically barred from signing the contract. We urgently need to enter into the contract with the winning supplier. What test does the court apply to an application to lift that automatic suspension, and realistically how quickly can we expect such an application to be dealt with?

We're defending a procurement challenge in the specialist construction and technology court, and the claimant's disclosure request would expose the winning bidder's confidential pricing information. How is this normally handled in practice, and does the winning bidder get any say given the claim is asking the court to unpick the award in its favour?

An internal audit has found that a council contract manager arranged for a favoured contractor to carry out unrelated work at his own property, and that same contractor went on to win a competitive tender the manager helped score. Beyond our procurement conflict-of-interest obligations, could the manager's conduct amount to a criminal offence, and what would a prosecutor be looking for?

We're thinking of setting up a dynamic market for temporary agency staff instead of running repeat tenders. What do we legally have to publish before we start, and what does the whole notice lifecycle from launch to closing the market actually look like?

We entered into a £2 million services contract three weeks ago under the Procurement Act 2023. By when do we have to publish the contract details notice, and is there anything we need to say in it about conflicts of interest?

On a major infrastructure contract, ground conditions we flagged in the tender notice as a possible problem have now actually caused delays that mean the contract can't be delivered as planned. Can we modify it to deal with this, and how do we make sure the change won't be successfully challenged?

We're a central government department with a £6m-a-year facilities contract that has significant sub-contracting below it. What are our payment-term obligations toward the subcontractors, and how are we meant to check the prime contractor is actually complying?

We published our OJEU-style contract notice under the old rules back in January 2025 but still haven't awarded the contract, now that the Procurement Act 2023 is fully in force. Do we carry on under the old Public Contracts Regulations, or do we now have to switch to the new Act?

We're planning some early conversations with the construction market before we tender a new build project. Do we have to publish anything about this before we start, and how far in advance should we give the market notice of an engagement event?

Our organisation has a live PCR2015-era contract, and the contractor is complaining that we're taking too long to pay their invoices, and that our terms don't clearly commit to paying subcontractors promptly either. What are we actually obliged to put in the contract on this, and what do we need to bear in mind operationally when checking whether we're compliant?

We're about to sign a £6 million services contract and want to set some KPIs for the supplier. Once the contract is live, what do we actually have to do to keep assessing and reporting on those KPIs over the life of the contract, and is that the same document we'd use if the supplier starts underperforming badly?

We're running a below-threshold procurement under the old regulations (the procurement started before the Procurement Act 2023 rules applied). Can we run a shortlisting/pre-qualification stage to cut down the number of bidders before we send out the tender documents, and if we can still ask suppliers some suitability questions, what constraints are we under?

We've just closed a Quick Quote exercise in Scotland for a below-threshold requirement and the responses are in. What's the practical process we should now follow, from opening the responses through to getting sign-off to award, and what should we do if a quote comes in with a price that looks suspiciously low or a supplier tries to attach their own terms and conditions?

We set up a dynamic purchasing system a few years ago under the old procurement rules and we're still using it to run mini-competitions, well after the Procurement Act's new rules took effect for everyone else. Is there a point at which we're legally forced to close it down or stop admitting new suppliers, or can we keep operating it under the old rules indefinitely?

We're a water company running a procurement under the utilities rules. We published our qualification-system notice and started inviting operators to register before the Procurement Act's rules took effect, but we haven't actually awarded anything under it yet. Someone in our team assumed that because the general public-sector procurement rules changed over, we now need to run everything from here on under the new Act. Is that right, or does something else govern how we finish this off?

We're procuring a leisure-centre operating concession. We submitted our concession notice for publication a little while before the Procurement Act rules came in, but we're only just getting to contract award now. Does the fact the notice went out before the change mean we carry on under the old concessions regime for the whole of this procurement, or do parts of it now have to follow the Act instead?

As a utility, we've been running an approved-supplier qualification system for years under the old utilities procurement rules, and we're still adding new suppliers to it. Now that the Procurement Act has been in force for a while, is there a deadline by which we have to stop admitting new suppliers to that list, or wind the whole thing up?

We set three KPIs on a £6m services contract as the Act requires. When we come to publish our first annual contract performance notice, do we have to report against all the KPIs we originally set, or can we just report against whichever ones we now think matter most?

We're an NHS integrated care board running a procurement under the health care provider selection regime. If the provider we're minded to award to says it plans to subcontract part of the service, do we have any legal duty to check whether that proposed subcontractor is on the debarment list, or is that only something we need to do for the provider itself?

A Ukrainian construction firm wants to bid into one of our tenders. Does the UK's non-discrimination duty toward 'treaty state suppliers' under the Procurement Act actually extend to Ukrainian suppliers, and on what legal basis?
For threshold purposes, if we're procuring installation of new drainage as part of a wider job, is that treated as a 'works' contract? Where do I actually find what counts as 'works'?

We want to run a competitive flexible procedure for a supply-of-nursing-staff contract and restrict it to public service mutuals only. Is nursing staff supply actually eligible to be reserved this way, and where's that confirmed?

We're continuing to run a dynamic purchasing system that we set up before the new procurement rules came in. Do we still have to keep it open to any supplier who meets the selection criteria throughout its life, or can we now close it to new entrants like a closed framework?

One of our evaluation panel members on a live tender (started under the old regime) has a close personal friendship with a director at one of the bidders. Is there a formal legal duty on us to do something about that, or is it just good practice?

For sustainable office furniture on a tender we're still running under the pre-2025 rules, can we require bidders to hold a specific eco-label, and can we reject a bid outright just because it doesn't have that exact label?
